title: Elements of AI — Chapter 2: AI problem solving
subtitle: How machines 'plan ahead' — state spaces, search, and games — in plain language.
attribution: Concepts follow Chapter 2 of the free 'Elements of AI' course (University of Helsinki & MinnaLearn, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). Original explanations generated for this app — not the course's text. Free course: https://course.elementsofai.com/2
audience: a smart non-technical operator of an automated ICT trading bot; tie examples to markets, order routing, and decision-making under uncertainty where natural, but keep the AI concepts front and centre.

episodes.title: Search & planning — the state space
episodes.focus: What 'AI problem solving' means: representing a problem as states + transitions; the state space; a search tree; a goal state; why 'planning ahead' IS search. Toy examples: route finding on a map, a simple sliding puzzle. Distinguish the state (a full snapshot), a transition (a legal move), and a path (a sequence of moves from start to goal).

episodes.title: Searching smart — cost, breadth vs depth, and heuristics
episodes.focus: How you actually explore a state space: breadth-first vs depth-first as two exploration orders; the combinatorial explosion (branching factor ^ depth) that makes exhaustive search infeasible; adding costs to transitions to find the CHEAPEST path (not just any path); the idea of a heuristic — a cheap estimate of 'how far to the goal' — to guide search toward good paths first (the intuition behind best-first / A*), without heavy math.

episodes.title: Games & adversaries — minimax and pruning
episodes.focus: Two-player games as adversarial search: a game tree where you and an opponent alternate moves; the minimax idea (assume the opponent always plays their best reply, so you maximise your worst case); why game trees explode even faster; the intuition behind pruning (alpha-beta) — skipping branches that can't change the decision; and why real engines lean on heuristics/evaluation functions + limited look-ahead instead of searching to the end.

sources:
Teach Chapter 2 of Elements of AI ('AI problem solving') from these concept notes — expand them into original, plain-language explanations; do NOT copy course text.

SECTION 2.1 — Search and problem solving.
- Many 'intelligent' tasks are really SEARCH: find a sequence of actions that turns a starting situation into a goal situation.
- STATE: a complete snapshot of the situation at one moment (e.g. the arrangement of tiles in a sliding puzzle; your location on a map; the full set of open positions + balances in a portfolio).
- TRANSITION / action: a legal way to move from one state to another (slide a tile; drive to an adjacent town; place/close an order). Transitions can have a COST (distance, time, fee).
- STATE SPACE: the set of ALL states reachable by applying transitions — usually astronomically large.
- SEARCH TREE: start at the initial state (root); each transition branches to a child state; a PATH from root to a GOAL state is a solution. 'Planning ahead' = finding such a path.
- Example: route finding. States = towns; transitions = roads (with distances); goal = destination; solution = the route. Example: 15-puzzle. States = tile arrangements; transitions = sliding the blank; goal = the ordered board.
- Key idea: represent the problem abstractly (states + transitions + goal test + costs), then let a general search procedure find the path — the same machinery solves many different problems.

SECTION 2.2 — Solving problems / exploring the state space.
- Two basic exploration orders. BREADTH-FIRST: explore all states one step away, then two steps away, ... — finds the shortest-in-#-moves path but can use a lot of memory. DEPTH-FIRST: follow one path as deep as possible, backtrack when stuck — light on memory but can wander down a bad branch.
- COMBINATORIAL EXPLOSION: with branching factor b and depth d, the number of paths grows like b^d. Even small b and d blow up fast, so brute-force 'try everything' is infeasible for real problems. This is THE central difficulty.
- COSTS: when transitions have costs, we usually want the CHEAPEST path, not just any path — so search must track accumulated cost (e.g. Dijkstra-style 'expand the cheapest-so-far frontier node').
- HEURISTICS: a heuristic is a cheap, approximate estimate of how far a state is from the goal (e.g. straight-line distance to the destination). Best-first / A*-style search uses it to explore promising states FIRST, so you find a good path without expanding the whole tree. A good heuristic never wildly over-estimates, so it can guide without misleading. Heuristics are how AI tames the explosion.

GAMES (adversarial search).
- A two-player, turn-taking game (tic-tac-toe, chess, checkers) is a GAME TREE: your move branches to states, then the OPPONENT moves, alternating to the end (win/lose/draw).
- MINIMAX: you can't assume the opponent helps you. You pick the move that MAXIMISES your outcome assuming the opponent will then MINIMISE it (play their best reply). You optimise your worst case. Values propagate up the tree: leaf outcomes → each level takes the max (your turn) or min (their turn).
- Game trees explode even faster than single-agent search (both players branch), so searching to the very end is impossible for non-trivial games.
- PRUNING (alpha-beta): while searching, you can prove some branches can't change the final choice (the opponent would never let you reach them, or you'd never choose them) and skip them entirely — same answer, far less work.
- REAL ENGINES: instead of reaching the end, they look ahead a limited number of moves and score the resulting positions with an EVALUATION FUNCTION (a heuristic for 'how good is this position'), then minimax over that shallow tree. Look-ahead depth + a good evaluation ≈ strong play.

THROUGHLINE for the audience: 'planning a sequence of actions under a huge number of possibilities, using estimates to avoid checking everything' is exactly the shape of many trading-system decisions (route a portfolio from its current state toward a target while an adversarial market moves against you) — but keep the teaching about the AI concepts; markets are just the running analogy.
